passage:
In the small kitchen in Lagos, Nkechi put her phone on the low stool. "No, Chidi. Don't touch."
Chidi, two, looked at her, then at the phone. His hand shot out at once. Nkechi moved it higher. He climbed onto the stool, reaching and shouting, "Mine!"
From the doorway, Yara, the neighbour, laughed. "He only wants it because you said no."
Nkechi handed him a wooden spoon and a pot lid. He banged them hard, the phone forgotten.

qa.q: Where did Nkechi first put her phone?
qa.a: Nkechi put her phone on the low stool.

qa.q: Why do you think Chidi reached for the phone right after hearing "No"?
qa.a: Being told not to touch made the phone seem more exciting 😊, and grabbing it let Chidi show he wanted to decide for himself.

qa.q: What worked for Nkechi in the end?
qa.a: Giving Chidi things he was allowed to use, a wooden spoon and a pot lid, so his push to do his own thing had a safe outlet.

qa.q: How does Yara see what is happening?
qa.a: Yara finds it funny and can see that Chidi only wants the phone because he was told no.

grounding: It shows a toddler reaching for something the moment he is told not to touch it, the ban making it more attractive.

passage: I'm Pradeep, and my little brother Siddharth is two. Yesterday Mummy said, "Siddharth, don't touch the tulsi pot." He hadn't even looked at it before. Right away he walked over and put both hands in the mud. Mummy said no again, louder. He looked back at her and patted the mud harder, smiling. I don't know what he was thinking. Maybe the pot just became the most interesting thing in the house.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do right after Mummy told him not to touch the tulsi pot?
qa.a: He walked over and put both hands in the mud.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's smile while patting the mud harder suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he may be enjoying doing things his own way; hearing no seemed to make the pot more interesting, though Pradeep can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Mummy try instead of saying no again?
qa.a: She could calmly move the pot out of reach and give Siddharth a small tub of mud or water he is allowed to play with.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see Siddharth's behaviour?
qa.a: Pradeep watches with curiosity rather than anger, guessing the pot became the most interesting thing once it was forbidden.

grounding: It shows a toddler going straight for a plant pot the moment he is told not to touch it, as noticed by an older sibling.

passage:
Monday: "No, Veer, not the diya," Neelam said. Veer, two, crawled straight to it, and she scooped him up just in time. He wailed and kicked.
Thursday: Neelam put the diya on the high shelf before evening and said nothing. Veer hardly looked at it.
Sunday: at Swati Masi's house he spotted a brass bell. Neelam said, "You can ring this one or bang the drum. You choose." Veer rang the bell hard, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Neelam put the diya on Thursday?
qa.a: Neelam put the diya on the high shelf before evening.

qa.q: Why did Veer crawl straight to the diya on Monday?
qa.a: Hearing no made the diya more tempting, and going for it anyway was Veer's way of showing he wanted to decide for himself.

qa.q: What changed in Neelam's approach that helped?
qa.a: She stopped saying no about dangerous things and simply moved them out of reach, then offered Veer a choice between safe things so he could still feel in charge.

qa.q: What would change if Neelam had kept saying "No, Veer" every evening?
qa.a: Veer would likely keep going for the diya, and each evening could turn into wailing and scooping him up in a hurry.

grounding: It shows a toddler reaching for a forbidden diya at once when told no, and how removing the ban and offering choices changes things.

passage: In their Mumbai flat, Arohi was colouring on the floor. "Mihir, don't touch my crayons," she said. Mihir, two, hadn't even noticed them. Now he crawled straight over and grabbed the red one, looking right at her. "No!" He grabbed two more and laughed. Hansa, their mother, said, "Arohi, give him one to hold." Mihir took the blue crayon and waddled off, happy. The rest stayed in the box.

qa.q: What did Mihir grab first?
qa.a: He grabbed the red one.

qa.q: Why did Mihir suddenly want the crayons?
qa.a: He hadn't noticed them until Arohi said no; being told not to touch made them exciting, and he wanted to show he could decide for himself.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that calmed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: She had Arohi give Mihir one crayon to hold, so he had something of his own and stopped grabbing the rest.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Mihir looked right at her and grabbed more?
qa.a: She might feel annoyed and teased, as if her little brother was doing it on purpose 😠

grounding: A toddler boy ignores crayons until he is told not to touch them, then grabs them at once to assert his own will.

passage:
"Om, don't touch Dadaji's spectacles," said Preeti, his mother.
Om, two, looked at the table. Then he toddled over and grabbed them with both hands.
"Om! No!"
"Mine!" He held them tighter.
Jagdish laughed from his chair. "The more you say no, the more he wants it. Give him something that's his." He held out a steel bowl and spoon. "Om, these are yours. Bang away."
Om dropped the spectacles and grabbed the spoon.
Preeti smiled and put the glasses on the high shelf. "Next time I'll just move them, Papaji."

qa.q: What did Jagdish hold out to Om?
qa.a: A steel bowl and spoon.

qa.q: Why did Om grab the spectacles right after Preeti said no?
qa.a: Being told not to touch made the spectacles more exciting, and shouting "Mine!" shows he wanted to do things his own way.

qa.q: What choice did Jagdish make that worked better than repeating no?
qa.a: He offered Om something that was his to use, so Om could still feel in charge and let go of the spectacles.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: She seems amused and a little relieved, and plans to simply move things out of reach next time rather than warn Om.

grounding: A toddler boy reaches for spectacles the moment he is told not to, showing how a ban makes a thing more tempting.
